summary: This standards-track document specifies mapping between X.400 messaging, as defined by ITU-T recommendations, and Internet mail in RFC 822 and MIME. It lets gateways translate messages between the two systems.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator who turns letters from one postal system into the other's format.

questions: how does x.400 map to rfc 822
what is an x.400 or address
subtitle: The rulebook for gateways that translate mail between X.400 and Internet RFC 822/MIME mail, covering addresses, headers and service elements.

tldr.problem: Internet mail (RFC 822 and MIME) and X.400 messaging use very different formats and address styles, yet users of one need to exchange mail with users of the other, possibly through several gateways.
tldr.mechanism: MIXER defines how a gateway maps an RFC 822 message and its SMTP information to an X.400 interpersonal message, and back. It covers a text form for X.400 addresses, new RFC 822 header fields for X.400 services, and the aim that mappings lose no information and can be reversed.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 987, 1026, 1138, 1148, 1327 and 1495, and it updates RFC 822. Body part mapping is left to the companion RFC 2157.

facts.label: Conversion loop limit
facts.value: More than 5 conversions in one direction means a loop

today: RFC 2156 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1998. It obsoletes RFC 987, RFC 1026, RFC 1138, RFC 1148, RFC 1327 and RFC 1495, and it updates RFC 822. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Two Mail Worlds
sections.content:
RFC 2156, called MIXER (Mime Internet X.400 Enhanced Relay), specifies a mapping between X.400 messaging and Internet mail. "X.400" here means the ITU-T 1988 and 1992 recommendations (ISO/IEC 10021). They define an Interpersonal Messaging System (IPMS) on top of a store-and-forward Message Transfer System. "RFC 822" means the combination of RFC 822 and MIME: a header plus a text body, with MIME adding a structured body. The core mapping works with any transfer protocol, and SMTP is covered in Appendix A.

The RFC says a large community uses RFC 822 mail and will want to reach X.400 users, and communities moving between the two technologies need conversion for a smooth transition. It expects more than one gateway, and wants them all to behave consistently. Here "gateway" means the component that does the mapping, which is the usual meaning among mail implementors.

The text lists design goals, which it says are not all achieved everywhere:

  • Be pragmatic, with no complex mappings for academic reasons.
  • Make functionality across a gateway as high as possible.
  • Avoid losing information, including requested services that cannot be fully mapped.
  • Understand the higher-level meaning of what is mapped.
  • Make mappings reversible, so a double transformation returns to the start.

It adds a warning: the rest of the document is technically detailed and will not make sense without knowing RFC 822 and X.400 (1988).
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups send each other letters but use different envelopes and writing styles. A translator in the middle has to turn each letter into the other style without losing anything important.

sections.title: The Gateway Model and Scenarios
sections.content:
On the X.400 side, the IPMS handles two kinds of object: the IPM (Interpersonal Message, made of a heading and a body of body parts) and the IPN (Interpersonal Notification). It sits on the Message Transfer System, whose messages carry an envelope with a message identifier, an originator and a list of recipients. On the RFC 822 side there is an underlying transfer service, usually SMTP, that identifies the recipients, gives an error return address and moves the message.

The RFC says the two sides do not line up neatly, so the mapping is "a slightly tangled" one. Going from RFC 822 to X.400, a message and its SMTP information always become an IPM, and a Delivery Status Notification becomes a Report. Going the other way, an IPN or an IPM can become an RFC 822 message, and a Report becomes a delivery status notification. Probes are processed by the gateway. Message contents of types other than those defined by the IPMS are not mapped and are rejected at the gateway if no other procedure exists.

The RFC describes two deployment cases. In the global scenario two global mail networks are joined by many gateways, and MIXER is critical. In the local scenario a gateway connects a closed community to a global network, and MIXER is useful. MIXER's conformance target is the global scenario. It notes that gateways meant for the local case tend to end up in the global one because of distribution lists and mail from non-customers.

Repeated crossings are supported, but the result tends toward the lowest common denominator, roughly what RFC 822 offers. The mapping uses the full X.400 (1988) rather than a 1984-compatible subset, with Appendix B for interworking with 1984 systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway is a border guard who opens each letter, rewrites it in the other country's format and passes it on. Some borders only serve one small town, and others connect the whole world.

sections.title: Service Elements Across a Gateway
sections.content:
Chapter 2 asks, for each feature a mail user can use, how well it survives the crossing. There are three levels: Supported (the protocol elements map well), Not Supported (a complete mismatch) and Partial Support. Supported means semantic correspondence, no significant loss of information, and any action the element requires.

Most RFC 822 headers map cleanly. Subject:, To:, Cc:, Bcc:, Reply-To: and Message-Id: are supported. Headers with no X.400 home, such as Keywords:, Comments: and any X-* or unknown field, are carried in a heading extension, which makes the information available but only partially supported.

In the other direction, X.400 services that RFC 822 cannot express get new RFC 822 header fields, registered by publication in this standard. Examples include Importance:, Sensitivity:, Expires:, Supersedes:, Autoforwarded:, Deferred-Delivery:, X400-Content-Type: and X400-MTS-Identifier:. The last is needed because X.400 has two message identifiers where RFC 822 has one.

Some services are simply not supported, notably the security services (content confidentiality, content integrity, message sequence integrity, proof of delivery and others). Unless stated otherwise, what happens to an unsupported element depends on its criticality marking: if it is marked critical for transfer or delivery, a non-delivery notification is generated, and otherwise the request is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Some parts of a letter, like the greeting and the subject, translate perfectly. Others have no matching word, so the translator sticks on a note that says what was meant.

sections.title: Mapping Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC calls addressing the most complex part of a gateway. An X.400 OR Address is an ordered set of attributes such as country (C), administration domain (ADMD), private domain (PRMD), organization (O), organizational units (OU) and personal name. MIXER defines a textual form, for example /I=J/S=Linnimouth/GQ=5/, that can be written in the local part of an RFC 822 address. A simpler form, Marshall.Rose or M.T.Rose, is allowed for common personal names.

Because the two namespaces are managed by different bodies, full global equivalence is not possible. MIXER instead defines a MIXER Conformant Global Address Mapping (MCGAM): an equivalence between a point in the Internet domain hierarchy and a point in the OR Address hierarchy (country, ADMD, PRMD, organization, then up to four organizational units). Everything below such a point maps one to one. The authority defining it must be responsible for both namespaces. MCGAMs can be published as text tables (Appendix F), through the DNS (RFC 2163) or through X.500 (RFC 2164).

The reverse direction uses a domain defined attribute with the type RFC-822. The RFC 822 address is written in printable string form, where for example @ becomes (a). A value is limited to 128 characters, and an address can use extra attributes RFC822C1 to RFC822C3 so that up to 512 characters can be encoded. Longer addresses cannot be encoded.

Addresses are designed to be reversible across a single gateway, so a reply can retrace the path. Source routing through the syntax is allowed but the RFC marks it as strongly discouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side writes addresses differently, like street-first versus city-first. The translator uses a conversion chart for places both sides agree on, and a special tag that says 'this is an address from the other side' for everything else.

sections.title: Translating Messages in Detail
sections.content:
Chapter 5 gives the field-by-field rules. Going from RFC 822 to X.400, a single IPM is generated from the message. The headers produce the IPMS heading, and fields that cannot be mapped go into an extension field holding a list of the original header lines, unfolded and without the trailing line break. The mapping of the body and of MIME headers is defined in RFC 2157.

Examples of the heading rules: To: becomes the primary recipients, Cc: the copy recipients, Reply-To: the reply recipients and Subject: the subject. Date: and Received: are not mapped into the heading but handled at the MTS and MTA levels. If a message has a Sender:, then From: goes to the authorizing users field and Sender: to the originator.

Going from X.400 to RFC 822, one RFC 822 message is generated from an IPM, report or notification. All body parts become a single RFC 822 body, and other services become header fields. The gateway must ensure minimal compliance: a Date: is always generated, From: defaults to the SMTP originator, and if there are no recipient fields, a field To: list:; is added.

Because conversion can defeat ordinary loop detection, gateways must count MIXER conversions, and if the count exceeds five in one direction the message is treated as if a loop was detected. A pseudo encoded information type, eit-mixer, marks that a conversion happened.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator goes through the letter line by line with a phrasebook. Lines with no match are copied over in a special box so nothing is lost, and the translator keeps a tally so a letter cannot bounce between the two sides forever.

sections.title: Conformance and Scope Limits
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit about what a conforming gateway must do. Subsets are non-conformant and strongly discouraged. The gateway must follow the field formats, enable MCGAMs, follow the formats for subject lines, delivery reports and notifications, implement all trace mappings, and follow RFC 2157 for body parts and RFC 2045 when it generates MIME. It must not follow RFC 1137 when mapping to SMTP.

A gateway must also state which transfer protocols it supports, which X.400 versions (84, 88, 92), and how it reaches MCGAMs (tables, X.500 or DNS). Optional parts include the extension mappings of Appendix C and returning illegal-format content in a delivery report.

It also lists what is not covered. MIXER does not extend RFC 822 to reach all X.400 services, and it is not an X.400 user interface. On the RFC 822 side the aim is to preserve current service, so the RFC says it would be a poor choice for X.400 implementors to use MIXER as an interface.

The document uses ISO wording, with "shall" for mandatory features and "may" for optional ones. To read it by Internet rules, replace each "shall" with "must".
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook says exactly what a good translator must do and what it does not have to do. It also says: do not use the translator as your everyday way to talk, because it only covers the common parts.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC has a one-line security section: security issues are not discussed in this memo. It does show security-related limits indirectly. The X.400 security services, such as content confidentiality, content integrity, message sequence integrity and proof of delivery, are listed as not supported across the gateway, so they cannot be relied on for a message that crosses it.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook does not say how to keep letters secret. The special seals and receipts that one side uses do not survive the trip through the translator.
